claim: The mechanosensing ability of lymphocytes regulates their activation in response to antigen stimulation.
source: The mechanosensing ability of lymphocytes regulates their activation in response to antigen stimulation, but the underlying mechanism remains unexplored.

claim: FAK inactivation or deficiency impaired B cell discrimination of substrate stiffness.

claim: The BCR is composed of a membrane-bound entity of immunoglobulin (Ig) and an Igα-Igβ heterodimer in a 1:1 stoichiometry.

evidence: This is supported by a citation to Pierce and Liu, 2010.

claim: B cell activation is remarkably sensitive to antigen density.

claim: B cell activation is remarkably sensitive to antigen affinity.

claim: B cell activation is remarkably sensitive to antigen valency.

claim: B cell activation is remarkably sensitive to Brownian mobility of the antigen.

source: Stiffness describes the extent that an object resists deformations in response to an applied force, which is quantified by Young's modulus in units of Pascal (Pa or N/m2 or m−1·kg·s−2) (Discher et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a definition supported by a citation to Discher et al., 2005.

evidence: This is supported by a citation to Mateu, 2012.

claim: B cells acquire extracellular matrix (ECM)-associated antigens in a B cell receptor (BCR) and contact-dependent manner.

claim: Carma1-KO DT-40 B cells effectively maintained their discrimination capability.

claim: PF573-228 pre-treated DT40 B cells were completely blunted in their capability to discriminate substrate stiffness.

claim: PF573-228 pre-treated CH27 B cells were completely blunted in their capability to discriminate substrate stiffness.

evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: PF573-228 pre-treated B1-8 primary B cells were completely blunted in their capability to discriminate substrate stiffness.

evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: DT40-FAK-KO B cells lost the capability to discriminate substrate stiffness during their activation.
source: To confirm this, we knocked out FAK in DT40 B cells (DT40-FAK-KO) using CRISPR/Cas9 gene editing technology (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–C) and found that DT40-FAK-KO B cells lost the capability to discriminate substrate stiffness during their activation.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 6E and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Exogenous expression of chicken FAK-WT rescued the capability of DT40-FAK-KO B cells to discriminate substrate stiffness.
source: This was rescued by the exogenous expression of chicken FAK-WT (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Exogenous expression of a chicken FAK-Y926F mutant in DT40-FAK-KO B cells failed to rescue the discrimination capability of B cells.
source: As expected, exogenous expression of a chicken FAK-Y926F mutant (chicken Tyr 926 has sequence homology with Tyr 925 in mouse and human FAK) (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D) in DT40-FAK-KO B cells failed to rescue the discrimination capability of B cells (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: BCRs primarily aggregated at the central region of the B cell IS, while pFAK accumulated at the peripheral region.
source: As predicted, BCRs primarily aggregated at the central region of the B cell IS, while pFAK accumulated at the peripheral region, consistent with the report that integrin molecules are mainly located at the peripheral region of the B cell IS (Tolar et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 6G and a citation to Tolar et al., 2009.

claim: No obvious upregulation of pFAK was observed in B cells that were placed on substrates without antigen coating.
source: Indeed, as further supporting evidence, we observed no obvious upregulation of pFAK in B cells that were placed on substrates without antigen coating, while very strong pFAK signaling was evident only in the antigen-activated B cells (Figure 6H).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 6H.

claim: A significantly stronger pFAK signal was observed in B cells that were placed on stiff substrates than in B cells on soft substrates.
source: Strikingly, a significantly stronger pFAK signal was observed in B cells that were placed on stiff substrates than in B cells on soft substrates (Figure 6I).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 6I.

claim: The ratio value of 2.5 for MFI of pFAK on stiff/soft PDMS substrates indicated that stiff substrates induced accumulation of significantly more pFAK molecules into the B cell IS compared with soft substrates.
source: The obtained ratio value of 2.5 for MFI of pFAK on stiff/soft PDMS substrates indicated that stiff substrates induced accumulation of significantly more pFAK molecules into the B cell IS compared with soft substrates (Figure 6J).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 6J.

claim: The activation of FAK was drastically impaired in DT40-PKCβ-KO cells compared with DT40-WT B cells.
source: As expected, the activation of FAK was drastically impaired in DT40-PKCβ-KO cells compared with DT40-WT B cells.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 6K.

claim: Exogenous PKCβ rescued the capability of B cells to accumulate pFAK in the B cell IS in response to BCR and antigen recognition.
source: Exogenous PKCβ rescued the capability of B cells to accumulate pFAK in the B cell IS in response to BCR and antigen recognition (Figure 6K).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 6K.

claim: DT40-PKCβ-KO B cells had a pFAK MFI ratio of only 1, suggesting that similar amounts of pFAK molecules accumulated at the contact interface of B cells on both stiff and soft PDMS substrates.
source: As mentioned above, further quantification using the pFAK MFI ratio index demonstrated that DT40-WT B cells exhibited a ratio value of 2.5; in marked contrast, DT40-PKCβ-KO B cells had a ratio of only 1, suggesting that similar amounts of pFAK molecules accumulated at the contact interface of B cells on both stiff and soft PDMS substrates (Figure 6J).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 6J.

claim: The pFAK MFI value was strongly correlated with the size of the B cell contact interface.
source: We found that the pFAK MFI value was strongly correlated with each of these three parameters (Figure 7B–D).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The pFAK MFI value was strongly correlated with the strength of B cell adhesion.
source: We found that the pFAK MFI value was strongly correlated with each of these three parameters (Figure 7B–D).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The pFAK MFI value was strongly correlated with the BCR MFI value.
source: We found that the pFAK MFI value was strongly correlated with each of these three parameters (Figure 7B–D).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: EDTA-treated B cells lost the capability to discriminate substrate stiffness.
source: EDTA-treated B cells lost the capability to discriminate substrate stiffness (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Splenic primary B cells from CD11a (ITGAL) knockout (KO) mice lost the capability to discriminate substrate stiffness.
source: Thus, to confirm this conclusion we used splenic primary B cells from CD11a (ITGAL) knockout (KO) mice, which lack the lymphocyte function-associated antigen 1 (LFA-1) (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: The addition of ICAM-1 significantly enhanced the B cell's capacity to discriminate between stiff and soft substrates.
source: The results showed that the addition of either ICAM-1 or VCAM-1 significantly enhanced the B cell's capacity to discriminate between stiff and soft substrates (Figure 8C–D,G).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 8C and 8G.

claim: The addition of VCAM-1 significantly enhanced the B cell's capacity to discriminate between stiff and soft substrates.
source: The results showed that the addition of either ICAM-1 or VCAM-1 significantly enhanced the B cell's capacity to discriminate between stiff and soft substrates (Figure 8C–D,G).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 8D and 8G.

claim: All the BCR MFI ratio index values were larger than 1 for human primary B cells from both healthy controls and RA patients.
source: The results showed that all the BCR (or pFAK) MFI ratio index values were larger than 1, indicating that all the human primary B cells from both healthy controls and RA patients exhibited substrate discrimination capabilities (Figure 9A–D).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 9A-D.

claim: B cells from RA patients exhibited a much weaker discrimination efficiency as indicated by the much lower BCR MFI ratio index, in comparison with B cells from the paired healthy controls.
source: However, careful examination of the BCR MFI ratio index values of the paired samples in the same batch of experiments revealed the presence of different efficiencies in terms of the capability of B cells to discriminate substrate stiffness: B cells from RA patients exhibited a much weaker discrimination efficiency as indicated by the much lower BCR (or pFAK) MFI ratio index, in comparison with B cells from the paired healthy controls (Figure 9A,B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 9A,B.

claim: This phenomenon was observed in six out of the nine paired samples examined.
source: We observed this phenomenon in six out of the nine paired samples that we examined (Figure 9—figure supplement 1A–F).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1A–F.

claim: In two pairs, a comparable B cell discrimination capability was observed in both the healthy control and RA patient.
source: In two pairs, we observed a comparable B cell discrimination capability in both the healthy control and RA patient (Figure 9—figure supplement 1G–H).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1G–H.

claim: In only one pair, B cells from the healthy control showed weaker discrimination capability than those from the RA patient.
source: In only one pair, B cells from the healthy control showed weaker discrimination capability than those from the RA patient (Figure 9—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1I.

claim: B cells from healthy controls preferentially enhanced the synaptic accumulation of BCR microclusters on stiff substrates.
source: The results showed that B cells from healthy controls preferentially enhanced the synaptic accumulation of BCR microclusters on stiff substrates.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 2A–I.

claim: RA patient B cells exhibited a different preference of mainly enhancing BCR accumulation on soft substrates.
source: In direct contrast, RA patient B cells preferentially enhanced BCR accumulation on soft substrates (Figure 9—figure supplement 2A–I).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 2A–I.

claim: Only BCR signaling-dependent, not BCR signaling-independent, accumulation of BCRs into the B cell IS is subjected to strict regulation by the mechanosensing capability of B cells.
source: The first striking observation was that only BCR signaling-dependent, not BCR signaling-independent, accumulation of BCRs into the B cell IS is subjected to strict regulation by the mechanosensing capability of B cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Btk and PLCγ2 function upstream of PKCβ in the pathway for B cell discrimination of substrate stiffness.
source: Together, these results suggest that Btk and PLCγ2 function upstream of PKCβ, demonstrating the key role of PKCβ in mediating the capability of B cells to discriminate substrate stiffness.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the manuscript, particularly the PMA rescue experiments.

claim: FAK activation is triggered by BCR engagement in a PKCβ-dependent manner.
source: Mechanistically, we found that FAK activation is triggered by BCR engagement in a PKCβ-dependent manner.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: PKCβ-dependent FAK activation accounts for B cell discrimination of stiffness by potentiating B cell spreading and adhesion responses.
source: Further colocalization analyses in this report indicated that pFAK mainly localized to the peripheral region of the B cell IS, and highly colocalized with F-actin, strongly suggesting that FAK activation supported B cell spreading and adhesion responses (Figure 9—figure supplement 1J). Indeed, additional analyses demonstrated that PKCβ-dependent FAK activation accounts for B cell discrimination of stiffness by potentiating B cell spreading and adhesion responses.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the manuscript, particularly the correlation analyses in Figure 7.

claim: B cells have evolved to maintain a high efficiency to discriminate substrate stiffness features because non-self-antigens presented by viral capsids usually exhibit a high degree of stiffness.
source: Firstly, we propose that B cells have evolved to maintain a high efficiency to discriminate substrate stiffness features because non-self-antigens presented by viral capsids usually exhibit a high degree of stiffness (45,000–1,000,000 kPa) (Mateu, 2012).
evidence: This is a speculative proposal based on the findings and cited literature.

claim: The findings provide a new explanation for the widely accepted observations in vaccine research that viral like particle (VLP) antigens are more potent than soluble antigens to induce antibody responses.
source: We believe that our findings here provide a new explanation for the widely accepted observations in vaccine research and administration that viral like particle (VLP) antigens are more potent than soluble antigens to induce antibody responses (Bachmann and Jennings, 2010; Bachmann et al., 1997, 1993).
